notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Nehemiah 7:50–73, drawn from the sources I was able to access:

---

## vv. 50–56 — The Nethinim (Temple Servants) continued

These verses complete the list of Nethinim families begun at v. 46. The term **Nethinim** means “given ones” (Hebrew *nᵉṯînîm*). They were temple assistants whose origin traces to the Gibeonites, whom Joshua conscripted as “hewers of wood and drawers of water” for the tabernacle (Joshua 9:27). Later, David and the princes supplemented them with prisoners of war and other slaves “given for the service of the Levites” (Ezra 8:20). Though they held a lowly place among temple personnel, they were exempt from taxes (Ezra 7:24), had their own quarters in Jerusalem’s Ophel district (Neh 3:26, 31), and took the oath of the covenant (Neh 10:28–31).

Thirty-two Nethinim families are listed here (thirty-five in Ezra 2); the three “missing” families (Akkub, Hagab, Asnah) were either accidentally omitted or subsumed into other clans. The small number of individuals per family suggests a relatively short ancestry. Many of the names are non-Israelite in origin, confirming their Gentile roots.

— Pett’s Commentary (studyLight.org, search excerpt)  
— biblehub.com/q on Nethinim role in Nehemiah 7:54, 56  
— enduringword.com

## vv. 57–59 — The Descendants of Solomon’s Servants

“Solomon’s servants” translates Hebrew *‘avdê Shelomoh*, a hereditary clan designation. Their origin is distinct from the Nethinim: Solomon conscripted the remaining Canaanite peoples (Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites) as a permanent forced-labour corps (1 Kings 9:20–22; 2 Chron 8:7–9). Over centuries, their descendants retained this occupational identity.

- **Nethinim** = dedicated by David to tabernacle/temple service.  
- **Solomon’s servants** = royal labour corps attached to temple and state projects.

Both groups functioned as temple aides. Rabbinic tradition (m. Middot 2:5) remembers their duties: gathering wood and water, cleaning courts, handling sacrificial by-products, and assisting Levites with gate supervision. In the acute manpower shortage of the return, these hereditary labourers made daily worship possible.

Two names hint at specialised duties: **Sophereth** (or Hassophereth) means “the scribes”; **Pochereth-hazzebaim** means “the gazelle-keepers.” The variant spellings between Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 (e.g., Peruda/Perida, Jaalah/Jaala, Ami/Amon) are minor and attributed to scribal variation.

— biblehub.com/q on Solomon’s servants in Neh 7:55  
— Pett’s Commentary (studyLight.org, search excerpt)  
— JFB Commentary (biblehub.com)

## v. 60 — Combined Total of Nethinim and Solomon’s Servants

“The temple servants and descendants of the servants of Solomon numbered 392 in all.”

The combined total of 392 is given for both groups together, indicating they were viewed as twin service orders with parallel functions. The numeric parity underscores God’s preservation of these marginalised servants for the worship of His house.

— Pett’s Commentary (studyLight.org, search excerpt)  
— biblehub.com/q on Nethinim in Neh 7:56

## vv. 61–62 — Those of Unproven Israelite Descent

“The following came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but could not prove that their families were descended from Israel: the descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah, and the descendants of Nekoda, 642 in all.”

These locations are Babylonian settlements where exiles had lived. The returnees from these places claimed Israelite ancestry but could produce no genealogical records to substantiate it. They could not “show their father’s house, nor their seed”—they could only say “we think we are.” Their inability to prove descent did not exclude them from the community of Israel entirely, but it did raise questions (resolved more severely for those claiming priestly descent in the next verses).

The number 642 is separate from the 42,360 total assembly (v. 66) and is not added into it.

— JFB, Clarke, Barnes (biblehub.com)  
— enduringword.com

## vv. 63–64 — Priests Excluded as Unclean

“And from among the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz, and the descendants of Barzillai (who had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name). These men searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean.”

Three priestly families could not document their Aaronic lineage. The case of **Barzillai** is especially noted: an ancestor had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite (the wealthy supporter of David, 2 Samuel 17:27–29; 19:31–39) and had taken the Barzillai name—a prestigious adoption that ironically now clouded his priestly pedigree. The phrase “excluded from the priesthood as unclean” (*defiled* or *polluted* in older translations) reflects that priestly service required proven descent from Aaron (Exodus 28:1; Numbers 3:10). Without verifiable records, these men could not serve, handle holy things, or eat the priestly portions. This was not a judgment on their personal character but a safeguarding of the holiness of the priestly office.

Ezra 2:62 records the identical exclusion, showing administrative consistency across nearly a century.

— biblehub.com/q on Neh 7:65 and priestly lineage  
— JFB, Clarke (biblehub.com)  
— enduringword.com

## v. 65 — The Governor’s Ruling and the Urim and Thummim

“The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim.”

**“The governor”**: Hebrew *Tirshatha*, a Persian title for the provincial governor. Commentators differ on whether this refers to **Zerubbabel** (the governor at the time of the first return, c. 537 BC) or **Nehemiah** (governor in 444 BC who discovered and reused the older register). The Poole/Matthew Henry tradition tends to identify him as Nehemiah; the Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary identifies him as Zerubbabel (studyLight.org).

**“Most holy things”** (*hakkōdāšîm haq-qodāšîm*): the portions of grain offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings reserved for priests alone (Leviticus 2; 6–7; Numbers 18:9–10). The excluded priests could eat ordinary food but not these consecrated portions.

**Urim and Thummim**: oracle stones kept in the high priest’s breastpiece (Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21). They were a means of receiving direct divine verdicts on matters that human records could not settle. Whether the Urim and Thummim survived the Babylonian captivity is unknown; Nehemiah’s statement “until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim” may anticipate its future restoration (JFB). The ruling demonstrates a dual principle: human documentation has limits, but divine revelation is sufficient. The community was to wait on God rather than take pragmatic shortcuts.

— JFB (biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/nehemiah/7.htm)  
— biblehub.com/q on Neh 7:65  
— studyLight.org verse-by-verse (JFB unabridged)

**A traditional homiletic application** (J. Vernon McGee style, seen in studyLight.org verse-by-verse): just as these men could not declare their genealogy and were “put from the priesthood,” a believer needs not only to be saved but to *know* he is saved. The Urim and Thummim pointed to God’s Word as the means of discerning what is genuine.  
— studyLight.org verse-by-verse commentary on Nehemiah 7:64–65

## vv. 66–67 — The Totals: People and Servants

“The whole assembly numbered 42,360, in addition to their 7,337 menservants and maidservants, as well as their 245 male and female singers.”

The total of 42,360 exceeds the sum of the individual numbers listed earlier (approximately 31,089 in Nehemiah 7; 29,818 in Ezra 2). Several explanations are given by commentators:

- Dr. Constable notes that both lists contain numerical discrepancies probably arising from scribal errors in copying Hebrew numerals, which were notoriously difficult to transmit (studyLight.org, Constable’s Expository Notes).
- Bible.org (Steven Cole) notes Derek Kidner’s observation that “half of the numbers disagree apparently at random, with sometimes one list and sometimes the other giving the larger figure”—a classic example of scribal difficulty with Hebrew numbers. The doctrine of inerrancy applies to the original manuscripts, not to every copy (bible.org).
- Others suggest the larger total includes women and children not enumerated in the individual clan counts.

The 7,337 servants and 245 singers (male and female) reflect that the returning community was not destitute. They brought a functioning household economy with them.

— Dr. Constable (studyLight.org)  
— bible.org (Steven Cole)  
— enduringword.com

## vv. 68–69 — Livestock

“They had 736 horses, 245 mules, 435 camels, and 6,720 donkeys.”

These numbers demonstrate that the returnees brought substantial wealth in the form of transport and pack animals. Horses (736) were a mark of status, mules (245) were valued riding and pack animals, camels (435) served long-distance caravan transport, and donkeys (6,720, the largest number) were the common beast of burden. The ratio of roughly one donkey per six persons suggests most families had at least one.

— JFB (biblehub.com)  
— enduringword.com

## vv. 70–72 — Contributions to the Work

These verses resume the narrative thread after the register ends (JFB notes that v. 69 closes the register and v. 70 resumes Nehemiah’s history). The giving is recorded in three tiers:

**v. 70 — The Governor.** “The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 darics of gold, 50 bowls, and 530 priestly garments.” A **daric** was a Persian gold coin weighing about 8.4 grams, valued at approximately £1 5s in older reckoning (JFB). The 50 **bowls** (or basins) were vessels used to receive the blood of sacrifices. The 530 **priestly garments** were needed because after decades in Babylon, no priestly vestments had been maintained for temple service (Gill). Gill notes this was a distinct collection from the one recorded in Ezra 2:69, made at a different time.

**v. 71 — Heads of Families.** “And some of the heads of the families gave to the treasury for the project 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver.” A **mina** (*maneh*) was 60 shekels, valued at about £9 or £7 10s in older reckoning (JFB, Gill).

**v. 72 — The Rest of the People.** “The rest of the people gave a total of 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 priestly garments.”

The total gifts differ from those recorded in Ezra 2:69. Two main explanations are offered: (1) one or both passages suffered textual corruption in transmission (Barnes, JFB); (2) the two passages record different collections—Ezra 2 records gifts at Zerubbabel’s time, while Nehemiah 7 records gifts at Nehemiah’s (or Ezra’s) time (Poole/Matthew Henry, Gill). The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** calculates the Tirshatha’s gift alone at approximately $270,000 in modern value, with the family heads’ and people’s gifts each exceeding $2,000,000 (studyLight.org).

In the ancient Near East, giving garments was a customary and honourable form of donation—conformable to prevailing sentiments and customs of society (JFB).

— JFB (biblehub.com)  
— Gill (biblehub.com)  
— Barnes (biblehub.com)  
— Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary (studyLight.org)  
— NET Bible notes (classic.net.bible.org)

## v. 73 — Settlement and Transition

“So the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, and temple servants, along with some of the people and the rest of the Israelites, settled in their own towns. And by the seventh month the Israelites had settled in their towns.”

This verse performs two functions:

**1. Closing the register.** The genealogical record served the practical purpose of guiding each family back to its ancestral town and property. Clarke notes that “the examination of the registers occupied about a month; for as soon as the walls were finished, which was in the sixth month (Elul), Nehemiah instituted the examination… and by the concluding verse we find that the different families had got into their paternal cities in the seventh month, Tisri.” The register “determined every thing: there was no room for complaint, and none to accuse the governor of partiality” (Clarke, biblehub.com).

**2. Transition to Nehemiah 8.** The seventh month (Tishri, corresponding to September/October) was the month of the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles. The last clause (“and by the seventh month the Israelites had settled in their towns”) sets the stage for the great assembly of Nehemiah 8. Barnes notes that in the Septuagint, the last two clauses of v. 73 stand as the beginning of Nehemiah 8. Dr. Constable observes that the “seventh month” here probably refers to Tishri in 537 BC (the year the exiles under Zerubbabel gathered to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles, cf. Ezra 3), though some apply it to 444 BC (Nehemiah’s time).

**Theological significance:** Enduring Word notes that the list “flows beautifully after the completion of the work because it reminds us that the work was really all about these people. The walls weren’t all that important; what was important was the benefit the walls provided for God’s people, enabling them to live in peace and security.” Bible.org (Steven Cole) adds, “The people in this list returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own city. They easily could have stayed in Babylon. Their families had been there for several generations. They were established and comfortable there… But they knew God’s promise to their forefather Abraham.”

— Clarke (biblehub.com)  
— Barnes (biblehub.com)  
— Dr. Constable (studyLight.org)  
— enduringword.com  
— bible.org (Steven Cole)

## Denominational Distinctives

On these particular verses, denominational differences are minor—most traditions handle this genealogical and financial material similarly:

- **Baptist** (Garner-Howes, studyLight.org): Identifies the Tirshatha in v. 70 as Zerubbabel, not Nehemiah. Computes modern monetary values for the gifts. Emphasises practical lessons: concern for placing the right persons in charge of the Lord’s work.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word, David Guzik): Emphasises the pioneer spirit of the returnees—only about 2% of exiled Jews returned. Stresses that individuals, families, and their gifts all matter to God. Draws applications about spiritual vigilance and the importance of knowing one’s spiritual identity.
- **Evangelical/Non-denominational** (Bible.org, Steven Cole): Emphasises five things that matter to God: worship, godly character, people, one’s place in God’s family history, and commitment to God’s purpose. Stresses that spiritual lineage (being born again) matters more than physical lineage for Christians.
- **Reformed/Anglican** (JFB, Ellicott, Barnes): Focus on historical-grammatical details—the value of darics and minas, the identity of the Tirshatha, the structure of the list and its relationship to Ezra 2.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan** (Clarke, Poole via biblehub.com): Clarke emphasises the practical fairness of the genealogical register: it eliminated complaints and prevented accusations of partiality against the governor. Poole identifies the Tirshatha as Nehemiah and sees this as a different collection from Ezra 2.
- **Lutheran and Catholic/Orthodox**: No distinct readings of these verses were found in the searches specific to lcms.org, 1517.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org.

---

## Other Views

**Modern scholarship** (biblehub.com Q&A pages; NET Bible notes): Notes the numerical discrepancies between Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, attributing them to scribal difficulties in copying Hebrew numerals. The NET Bible notes that “darics” (v. 70) is the correct rendering for the gold coins. Archaeology—including Persian-period Yehud stamp impressions, Elephantine papyri (407 BC), and bullae inscribed with names matching the list (e.g., “Temah,” “Sophereth”)—corroborates the historical plausibility of this roster.

**Catholic/Orthodox**: The search did not yield specific commentary on these verses from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org. These traditions generally read this passage historically, viewing the concern for priestly lineage (vv. 63–65) as consistent with the Catholic understanding of apostolic succession and the holiness of ordained ministry.

**Word of Faith / Prosperity**: No distinct prosperity-gospel reading of these verses surfaced in the searches.
